title.value: Endoscopic Management of Bronchopleural Fistulas || source_page: 1 || source_excerpt: "Endoscopic Management of Bronchopleural Fistulas"

diagnostic_approaches.name: Modified Le Brigand classification
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Categorize BPF after pneumonectomy by onset timing
criteria_or_scoring: late: occurring more than 30 days post-surgery
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Assigns BPF to early, intermediate, or late categories based on days after surgery.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: After pneumonectomy, based on time of onset.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: early (within 1–7 days post-surgery), intermediate (between 8 and 30 days post-surgery), and late (occurring more than 30 days post-surgery).

diagnostic_approaches.name: Chest radiograph
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Initial imaging to evaluate suspected BPF
criteria_or_scoring: decreasing air-fluid levels ≥2 cm over time.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Appearance of new air-fluid planes/tension pneumothorax or decreasing air-fluid levels ≥2 cm suggests BPF.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Most patients with symptoms compatible with a BPF are initially evaluated with chest radiograph.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Strong indicators for a BPF are the appearance of new air-ﬂuid planes, the development of a tension pneumothorax and decreasing air-ﬂuid levels ≥2 cm, over time, indicating pleural ﬂuid displacement.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Chest CT (computed tomography)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identify abnormalities related to BPF
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: May not identify the exact fistula location; localized site found in only 50% in a small study.
limitations: Likely will not identify the location of the fistula itself.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: In patients with clinical suspicion for BPF.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: the ﬁstula site could be isolated on CT scans in only 50% of the patients.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Flexible bronchoscopy (direct visualization)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Visualize central/large BPFs and examine surgical stump
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Perform bronchoscopy; inspect stump; attempt direct visualization of fistula opening.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: In large or central lesions, fistula opening may be directly visualized.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Should be performed in all patients suspected of having a BPF.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Bronchoscopy should be performed in all patients suspected of having a BPF.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Saline instillation onto stump (bronchoscopic bubbling test)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Detect postoperative stump leak indicating BPF
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Instill saline onto the surgical stump during bronchoscopy.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Continuous bubbling of saline from the stump indicates a fistula is present.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Suspected postoperative BPF when stump dehiscence is not seen.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: continuous bubbling of saline from the stump indicates a ﬁstula is present (Fig. 3).

diagnostic_approaches.name: Methylene blue instillation test (stump or retrograde)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Confirm presence of BPF via dye detection
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Instill methylene blue onto stump; or administer retrograde into thoracic drainage under bronchoscopic observation.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Presence of dye in chest tube output indicates a BPF.
limitations: Dye may affect in situ tissue discriminability if subsequent surgery is required.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: In the immediate postoperative patient, installation of methylene blue onto stump can be performed. Its presence in the chest tube output indicates a BPF is present.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchoscopic balloon occlusion with chest tube leak observation
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Localize peripheral BPF by occluding suspect airway
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Insert balloon via bronchoscope into suspected segment; inflate to occlude airflow; observe waterseal chamber for change.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Air leak decreases or disappears if the targeted segment contains a fistula; no impact if it does not.
limitations: More than one airway may contribute
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: In patients with a chest tube; start with larger airways if location unknown.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Once inﬂated, the balloon will occlude airﬂow through the ﬁstula, and therefore, the air leak will decrease or disappear in the waterseal chamber of a pleural collection device.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Chartis System (airway pressure/flow measurement)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identify airways involved in BPF by pressure behavior distal to occlusion
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Navigate to target airway; inflate balloon catheter to occlude; measure distal pressure/flow.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: If pressure remains negative during both inspiration and expiration, a BPF is present.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Useful when no chest tube or when waterseal bubbling changes are subtle during balloon occlusion.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: If the pressure remains negative during both inspiration and expiration, a BPF is present.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Capnography via bronchoscope
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Localize the segment with BPF by exhaled CO2 absence
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Place polyurethane catheter attached to capnometer through bronchoscope into sequential airways.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Absence of an end tidal CO2 tracing in a segment identifies the segment with the fistula.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Useful without chest tubes or when bubbling changes are subtle during balloon occlusion.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The absence of an end tidal CO2 tracing in a particular segment identiﬁes the segment with the ﬁstula as the carbon dioxide leaks out into the pleural space.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchography with iodinated contrast
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Confirm and localize BPF when other bronchoscopic methods are inconclusive
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Inject 20–30 mL water-based nonionic low osmolar iodinated contrast via bronchoscope; perform fluoroscopy or CT.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Extravasation of contrast material into pleural space indicates BPF.
limitations: Now infrequently used with advent and safety of balloon occlusion.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: If abovementioned bronchoscopic techniques are inconclusive.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: In bronchography, 20–30 mL of a water-based nonionic low osmolar iodinated contrast medium (i.e., Omnipaque, GE Healthcare) is injected through a catheter placed through the working channel of a bronchoscope

diagnostic_approaches.name: Scintigraphy with 99mTc-albumin colloid fog inhalation
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Detection of BPF
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Aerosolize radiotracer and inhale; accumulation occurs at BPF location.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Accumulation of radiotracer at BPF site indicates presence.
limitations: can be inconclusive with small fistulas or COPD.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Scintigraphy with 99mTc-albumin (technetium-albumin) colloid fog inhalation has been described as a simple and accurate test for the detection of BPF.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Ventilation scintigraphy with alternative tracers
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Alternative nuclear ventilation imaging for BPF detection
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: ventilation scintigraphy with other radioactive tracers such as 81mKr (Krypton), 133Xe (Xenon), 99mTc-DTPA (technetium-labeled diethylenetriamine penta-acetate), and 99mTc-sulfur colloid has also been described.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Chest tube waterseal observation
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Alert to possible BPF after thoracic surgery
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Observe for continuous air leak or increased air output in waterseal chamber.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Such findings should alert to possibility of BPF.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Immediate postoperative period in thoracic surgery patients with chest tubes.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: A continuous air leak or increase in the output of air in the waterseal chamber of a pleural ﬂuid collection container

diagnostic_approaches.name: Airway pressure monitoring on mechanical ventilation
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Raise suspicion for BPF formation
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Monitor airway pressures on mechanical ventilation.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Abrupt and significant decrease in airway pressures should raise concerns for BPF.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: In patients on mechanical ventilation, an abrupt and signiﬁcant decrease in airway pressures should raise concerns for BPF formation.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchoscopy (diagnostic visualization for BPF)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Visualize airway/surgical stump to detect a central BPF or identify the involved airway in a peripheral BPF.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use a flexible bronchoscope to visualize the airway and/or surgical stump for evidence of a central BPF or to identify the airway leading to a peripheral BPF.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Examine for a central BPF or identify the involved airway in a peripheral BPF.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Indicated in all patients with a BPF.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Bronchoscopy is indicated in all patients with a BPF.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Balloon occlusion under bronchoscopy for localization
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Localize the airway segment leading to a BPF when not seen centrally.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Identify the involved segment by systematically inflating a balloon during bronchoscopy.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When the fistula is not seen in the central airways.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Initially, the bronchoscope is used to identify the involved segment by systematically inflating a balloon as described above.

diagnostic_approaches.name: BPF size classification for endoscopic closure suitability
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Categorize BPFs by size to assess likelihood of success with endoscopic closure.
criteria_or_scoring: Small (<5 mm) vs large (>8 mm) fistulas.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Small (<5 mm) are more likely to be successfully treated endoscopically; large (>8 mm) are not suitable for endoscopic closure alone.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Small (<5 mm) fistulas are more likely to have successful treatment endoscopically, whereas large fistulas (>8 mm) are not suitable for endoscopic closure alone.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Early versus late BPF classification
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Distinguish early post-resection BPF without empyema from late BPF due to empyema/pleuropulmonary disease to guide approach.
criteria_or_scoring: Early: after lung resection without empyema. Late: due to empyema and/or pleuropulmonary disease.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Early: rapid fistula closure should be attempted. Late: a conservative approach over several weeks may be necessary.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: a distinction should be made between early BPF after lung resection without empyema, in which rapid fistula closure should be attempted, and late BPF due to empyema and/or pleuropulmonary disease

diagnostic_approaches.name: Central versus peripheral BPF classification via bronchoscopy
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Classify BPF location as central or peripheral during bronchoscopy.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Bronchoscopic visualization of the airway/surgical stump to determine central vs peripheral involvement.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Determines whether a fistula is central or identifies the involved airway in a peripheral BPF.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: visualization of the airway and/or surgical stump to examine for a central BPF or to identify the involved airway in a peripheral BPF

diagnostic_approaches.name: Criterion: distal, small BPF <6 mm endoscopic closure success
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Quantify endoscopic closure potential for small distal BPFs.
criteria_or_scoring: <6 mm distal BPFs considered for endoscopic closure.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Endoscopic closure successful in 71.4–92.3% of such cases.
limitations: Based on a retrospective case series.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When evaluating small distal BPFs for endoscopic closure.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: distal, small BPF <6 mm can be closed endoscopically in 71.4–92.3% of cases

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchoscopy
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Helpful in diagnosis of BPF
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Can be helpful in both diagnosis and treatment of the BPF.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Indicated in all patients with BPF
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Bronchoscopy is indicated in all patients with BPF and can be helpful in both diagnosis and treatment of the BPF.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Balloon catheter-directed occlusion of subsegmental airways
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identify a peripheral air leak
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Balloon catheter-directed occlusion of subsegmental airways
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Used diagnostically to identify a peripheral air leak.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: As described earlier, balloon catheter-directed occlusion of subsegmental airways is used diagnostically to identify a peripheral air leak.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Chest CT assessment of collateral ventilation
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Assess collateral ventilation relevant to BPF closure with valves
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Findings relate to the effectiveness of endobronchial valve placement for prolonged air leak.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: In the context of BPF closure with valves
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: ventilation on Chest CTs. These results suggest that endo- bronchial valve placement appears to be a safe and effective

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bathel score
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identified as a risk factor for therapy failure in EWS outcomes
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Low Bathel score associated with treatment failure.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The main risk factors for therapy failure were age >85 years, male sex, low Bathel score, interstitial pneumonia, antibiotic and steroid treatment

clinical_guidelines.title: Early postoperative management of bronchopleural fistula
specific_recommendations: Bronchopleural fistulas identified within the first 4 days postoperative should return for re-exploration and closure of the stump leak if clinical situation allows.
decision_points_and_pathways: Identify BPF within first 4 days post-surgery -> return for re-exploration and stump closure if clinically feasible
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Postoperative patients with BPF identified within the first 4 days after surgery
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Bronchopleural fistulas identified within the first 4 days postoperative should return for re-exploration and closure of the stump leak if clinical situation allows.

clinical_guidelines.title: Bronchoscopic evaluation for suspected bronchopleural fistula
specific_recommendations: Bronchoscopy should be performed in all patients suspected of having a BPF.
In the case of a suspected postoperative BPF, the stump should be closely examined.
If stump dehiscence is not seen, saline should be instilled onto the stump.
In the immediate postoperative patient, installation of methylene blue onto stump can be performed.
Retrograde administration of methylene blue into the thoracic drainage under bronchoscopic observation can be performed.
decision_points_and_pathways: Suspected BPF -> perform bronchoscopy
If central lesion visible -> direct visualization confirms fistula
If stump dehiscence not seen -> instill saline; continuous bubbling indicates fistula
Option: methylene blue on stump or retrograde via thoracic drainage under bronchoscopic observation
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: All patients suspected of having a bronchopleural fistula; postoperative patients with suspected stump leak
contraindications_and_exceptions: The presence of the dye may affect the in situ tissue discriminability if subsequent surgery is required.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Bronchoscopy should be performed in all patients suspected of having a BPF.

clinical_guidelines.title: Balloon occlusion technique to localize peripheral bronchopleural fistula
specific_recommendations: Insert a balloon via the bronchoscope into the segment or subsegment with suspected fistula.
Once inflated, occlude airflow; air leak will decrease or disappear in the waterseal chamber if target segment contains fistula.
If the segment does not contain a fistula, balloon inflation has no impact on the air leak.
If general location unknown, inflate a larger balloon in larger airways before proceeding to segmental bronchi.
Multiple balloon inflations may be necessary if more than one airway contributes to a fistula.
decision_points_and_pathways: Suspected peripheral BPF with chest tube -> segmental balloon occlusion -> observe air leak change
No change -> move to other segments
Unknown general location -> start with larger airway balloon, then proceed segmentally
Multiple culprit airways -> repeat balloon occlusions
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with suspected peripheral BPF, typically with chest tube in place
monitoring_requirements: Observe decrease or disappearance of air leak in the waterseal chamber of a pleural collection device during balloon occlusion
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Once inﬂated, the balloon will occlude airﬂow through the ﬁstula, and therefore, the air leak will decrease or disappear in the waterseal chamber of a pleural collection device.

clinical_guidelines.title: Use of Chartis system for bronchopleural fistula identification
specific_recommendations: With balloon-occluded airway, measure distal pressure/flow using Chartis.
If the pressure remains negative during both inspiration and expiration, a BPF is present.
decision_points_and_pathways: Occlude target airway with Chartis balloon -> assess distal pressure/flow
Negative pressure during inspiration and expiration -> indicates BPF in the segment
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients undergoing bronchoscopic localization of BPF
monitoring_requirements: Monitor airway pressure and flow distal to the occluded bronchus during Chartis measurement
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: If the pressure remains negative during both inspiration and expiration, a BPF is present.

clinical_guidelines.title: Capnography-based localization of bronchopleural fistula
specific_recommendations: Place a polyurethane catheter attached to a capnometer through the bronchoscope into sequential airways.
During exhalation, end tidal CO2 should be detected; absence identifies the segment with the fistula.
decision_points_and_pathways: Sequentially sample segments with capnography
Absent end tidal CO2 tracing in a segment -> identifies airway with fistula
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with suspected BPF where localization is needed, including without chest tubes
monitoring_requirements: Monitor end tidal CO2 tracings during exhalation for each sampled segment
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The absence of an end tidal CO2 tracing in a particular segment identiﬁes the segment with the ﬁstula as the carbon dioxide leaks out into the pleural space.

clinical_guidelines.title: Bronchography when bronchoscopic techniques are inconclusive
clinical_guidelines.condition: Suspected bronchopleural fistula with inconclusive bronchoscopic localization
specific_recommendations: Inject 20–30 mL of a water-based nonionic low osmolar iodinated contrast medium via bronchoscope.
Perform fluoroscopy or CT to visualize extravasation from a BPF site.
decision_points_and_pathways: Bronchoscopic techniques inconclusive -> proceed to bronchography with contrast injection
Imaging shows contrast extravasation -> confirms BPF location
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with suspected BPF where prior bronchoscopic techniques are inconclusive
alternative_approaches: Advanced radiographic techniques are now infrequently used with the advent and safety of balloon occlusion of the airway
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: In bronchography, 20–30 mL of a water-based nonionic low osmolar iodinated contrast medium (i.e., Omnipaque, GE Healthcare) is injected through a catheter placed through the working channel of a bronchoscope

clinical_guidelines.title: Ventilation scintigraphy for detection of bronchopleural fistula
specific_recommendations: Scintigraphy with 99mTc-albumin colloid fog inhalation has been described as a simple and accurate test for detection of BPF.
decision_points_and_pathways: Consider ventilation scintigraphy when other methods are inconclusive or not feasible
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Non-intubated patients able to cooperate with inhalation scintigraphy
contraindications_and_exceptions: Technique can be inconclusive in small fistulas or underlying lung disease such as COPD
Requires substantial time and cooperation in non-intubated patients
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Scintigraphy with 99mTc-albumin (technetium-albumin) colloid fog inhalation has been described as a simple and accurate test for the detection of BPF.

clinical_guidelines.title: Radiographic indicators and initial imaging for suspected BPF
specific_recommendations: Most patients with symptoms compatible with a BPF will initially be evaluated with a chest radiograph.
Strong indicators for a BPF include new air-fluid planes, tension pneumothorax, and decreasing air-fluid levels ≥2 cm over time.
decision_points_and_pathways: Initial chest radiograph -> assess for strong indicators (new air-fluid planes, tension pneumothorax, decreasing air-fluid levels ≥2 cm)
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with symptoms compatible with a bronchopleural fistula
alternative_approaches: Chest CT is more sensitive at identifying abnormalities related to a BPF
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Strong indicators for a BPF are the appearance of new air-ﬂuid planes, the development of a tension pneumothorax and decreasing air-ﬂuid levels ≥2 cm, over time, indicating pleural ﬂuid displacement.

clinical_guidelines.title: Modified Le Brigand classification for timing of postoperative BPF
specific_recommendations: Early: within 1–7 days post-surgery.
Intermediate: between 8 and 30 days post-surgery.
Late: occurring more than 30 days post-surgery.
decision_points_and_pathways: Categorize postoperative BPF by timing: early (1–7 days), intermediate (8–30 days), late (>30 days)
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: early (within 1–7 days post-surgery), intermediate (between 8 and 30 days post-surgery), and late (occurring more than 30 days post-surgery).

clinical_guidelines.title: Initial management of bronchopleural fistula (General Principles)
specific_recommendations: Address immediate, life-threatening conditions (pleural space contamination, pulmonary flooding, tension pneumothorax).
Insert a chest tube immediately if not already in place.
In complex cases with pleural adhesions and/or loculated hydropneumothoraces, use multiple well-positioned and/or image-guided chest tubes.
For BPF due to necrotizing lung or pleural space infection, attempt antibiotics with adequate drainage to decompress the pleural space to allow lung re-expansion and fistula healing.

With severe necrotizing pneumonia, many weeks of antibiotic therapy, nutritional supplementation, patient rehabilitation, and chronic pleural space drainage may be required before contemplating surgery.
Avoid acute surgical closure when there is active infection in the lung parenchyma or pleural space, as it can lead to worse outcomes.
decision_points_and_pathways: If immediate life-threatening conditions are present, insert a chest tube immediately.
If pleural adhesions/loculated hydropneumothoraces are present, consider multiple and/or image-guided chest tubes.
If BPF is due to necrotizing infection, prioritize antibiotics and drainage before considering surgery.
If severe necrotizing pneumonia is present, delay surgery while providing prolonged antibiotics, nutrition, rehabilitation, and drainage.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Active infection in the lung parenchyma or pleural space can lead to worse outcomes in the acute setting.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The initial management of any BPF should first address any immediate, life-threatening conditions, such as pleural space contamination, pulmonary flooding, or tension pneumothorax.

clinical_guidelines.title: Conservative therapy for BPF on mechanical ventilation and chest tube management
specific_recommendations: Limit airway pressure; minimize PEEP, inspiratory flow rate, and tidal volume to the extent tolerated.
For large fistulas, selective intubation of the contralateral lung may be necessary.
High-frequency oscillatory ventilation may be slightly more beneficial in proximal BPF with lack of parenchymal disease.
In minimal or no residual pneumothorax, remove suction and place the chest tube on water seal.
Withdraw suction from chest tubes to minimize airflow through the fistula and improve healing.
Consider pleural sclerosing agents (e.g., talc, bleomycin) via chest tube; pleurodesis requires the lung to completely fill the hemithorax.
If a large pneumothorax is present, pleurodesis will not be achieved and the air leak will persist.
Differentiate early BPF after lung resection without empyema (attempt rapid closure) from late BPF due to empyema/pleuropulmonary disease (may require a conservative approach over several weeks).
decision_points_and_pathways: Large fistula: consider selective intubation of the contralateral lung.
Minimal/no residual pneumothorax: remove suction and place chest tube on water seal.
Large pneumothorax: pleurodesis will not be achieved; air leak persists.
Early post-resection BPF without empyema: attempt rapid closure; Late BPF with empyema/pleuropulmonary disease: pursue conservative therapy over weeks.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with BPF on mechanical ventilation.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Pleurodesis is ineffective if the lung does not completely fill the hemithorax (e.g., large pneumothorax present).
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: suction should be removed and the chest tube placed on water seal.

clinical_guidelines.title: Surgical closure of early postoperative BPF (re-exploration)
specific_recommendations: If a postoperative BPF is detected within a few days of the original surgery, re-exploration by VATS or open thoracotomy with closure is recommended if the clinical situation allows.
decision_points_and_pathways: Postoperative BPF detected within a few days: re-explore by VATS or open thoracotomy with closure if clinically appropriate.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Postoperative BPF detected within a few days of the original surgery.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Proceed only if the clinical situation allows.
clinical_guidelines.outcome_measures: The success rate of BPF closure with surgery has been reported to be as high as 80–95%.
clinical_guidelines.alternative_approaches: Endoscopic closure may be considered as a complementary technique.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The success rate of BPF closure with surgery has been reported to be as high as 80–95%,

clinical_guidelines.title: Surgical options and staged approach including Eloesser procedure
specific_recommendations: Surgical options: VATS/thoracotomy with direct resection and stump closure with intercostal muscle reinforcement or omental flap; trans-sternal bronchial closure; thoracoplasty with/without extrathoracic chest wall muscle transposition; chronic drainage with chest tube or Eloesser procedure.
Plan sequential operations in debilitated patients who would not tolerate another major operation.
For BPF with empyema, sequential operations may achieve better success.
Eloesser procedure: create chest wall opening with rib resection and suture skin to pleural cavity for continuous drainage; minimal morbidity; usable in the acute setting.
After recovery, return for thoracotomy with flap closure of the BPF.
decision_points_and_pathways: Debilitated or empyema-complicated BPF: employ staged approach with initial drainage (e.g., Eloesser), then definitive closure once patient is nutritionally and functionally improved.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Debilitated patients or BPF complicated by empyema.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: It involves the creation of a 5-cm opening in the chest wall with resection of two to three adjacent ribs and suturing of the skin to the pleural cavity

clinical_guidelines.title: Endoscopic management: role of bronchoscopy and indications
specific_recommendations: Bronchoscopy is indicated in all patients with a BPF.
Use bronchoscopy to visualize central BPFs or identify involved airway in peripheral BPF.
Bronchoscopic closure is indicated in patients at high risk for direct surgery (hemodynamic instability, severe hypoxemia, advanced malignancy).
Consider two-staged management: initial endoscopic closure during acute illness, followed by surgical fixation when the patient is improved.
Endoscopic and surgical treatments are complementary, not competing.
decision_points_and_pathways: High-risk for surgery (e.g., hemodynamic instability, severe hypoxemia, advanced malignancy): attempt bronchoscopic closure initially, then consider surgery when feasible.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients at high risk for direct surgery (hemodynamic instability, severe hypoxemia, advanced malignancy).
clinical_guidelines.outcome_measures: Distal, small BPF <6 mm can be closed endoscopically in 71.4–92.3% of cases.
clinical_guidelines.alternative_approaches: Surgical repair as a complementary technique.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: A retrospective case series has shown that distal, small BPF <6 mm can be closed endoscopically in 71.4–92.3% of cases,

clinical_guidelines.title: Endoscopic tissue sealants and glues: size-based suitability and approach
specific_recommendations: For nonsurgical candidates, apply sealant material to the airway defect via bronchoscope.
Small (<5 mm) fistulas are more likely to be successfully treated endoscopically.
Large (>8 mm) fistulas are not suitable for endoscopic closure alone.
Identify the involved segment using balloon occlusion and apply sealant/glue via catheter.
decision_points_and_pathways: If the fistula is not seen in central airways, occlude the segmental/subsegmental airway leading to the BPF to cease airflow and allow closure.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Nonsurgical candidates requiring minimally invasive endoscopic closure.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Large fistulas (>8 mm) are not suitable for endoscopic closure alone.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Small (<5 mm) fistulas are more likely to have successful treatment endoscopically, whereas large fistulas (>8 mm) are not suitable for endoscopic closure alone.

clinical_guidelines.title: One-way endobronchial valves for prolonged air leaks
specific_recommendations: Use one-way endobronchial valves to allow unidirectional air and secretion flow out of the lung parenchyma but not back in, minimizing air leak and permitting potential closure.
The Spiration system has FDA compassionate human use approval for prolonged air leaks.
decision_points_and_pathways: Prevent airflow back through the affected airway to minimize the leak and allow eventual fistula closure.
clinical_guidelines.alternative_approaches: Other endoscopic options (e.g., tissue sealants) or surgical repair.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: It has been approved for compassionate human use in the United States by the FDA since 2008 (HO60002) for prolonged air leaks.

specific_recommendations: Consider valve removal after 6 weeks after placement or upon resolution of the air leak to minimize long-term airway complications.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: It is recommended to start considering valve removal after 6 weeks after placement o upon resolution of the air leak

figures.title: Bronchoscopic localization of a peripheral BPF.
figures.caption: Fig. 4 Bronchoscopic localization of a peripheral BPF. Inﬂating a balloon within airway leading to a BPF will stop airﬂow into effected airway. This will either (1) slow or stop the air leak in water seal chamber of pleural collection system or (2) lead to a persistent negative pressure measured by the Chartis™system
key_findings: Inflating a balloon within the airway leading to a BPF will stop airflow into the affected airway.
This will either slow or stop the air leak in the water seal chamber or lead to a persistent negative pressure measured by the Chartis system.
figures.clinical_significance: Balloon occlusion helps localize a peripheral BPF by altering air leak or airway pressure.
figures.source_excerpt: Fig. 4 Bronchoscopic localization of a peripheral BPF.

figures.title: Chartis™ system developed for endoscopic LVRS can be helpful in localizing a BPF.
figures.caption: Fig. 5 Chartis™system developed for endoscopic LVRS can be helpful in localizing a BPF. The balloon is inﬂated and a pressure sensor at the end of the balloon measures both pressure and ﬂow distal to the occluded bronchus. A signiﬁcant negative pressure during both inspiration and expiration indicates a segment involved in a BPF. (© 2010 Pulmonox. All Rights Reserved)
key_findings: Chartis system can be helpful in localizing a BPF.
Balloon inflation with a pressure sensor measures pressure and flow distal to the occluded bronchus.
Significant negative pressure during inspiration and expiration indicates a segment involved in a BPF.
figures.clinical_significance: Helpful in localizing a bronchopleural fistula.

definitions.content: A bronchopleural ﬁstula (BPF) is an abnormal communication between a proximal airway, that is, a main stem, a lobar or a segmental bronchus, and the pleural space.
definitions.source_excerpt: A bronchopleural ﬁstula (BPF) is an abnormal communication between a proximal airway

definitions.content: The Eloesser procedure was named after Leo Eloesser, the thoracic surgeon who ﬁrst described the technique. It involves the creation of a 5-cm opening in the chest wall with resection of two to three adjacent ribs and suturing of the skin to the pleural cavity to allow complete continuous drainage of the pleural space.
definitions.source_excerpt: It involves the creation of a 5-cm opening… resection of two to three adjacent ribs… continuous drainage of the pleural space.

definitions.content: The Spiration valve is a one-way umbrella-shaped endobronchial valve that is deployed via a flexible bronchoscope. It allows for unidirectional air and secretion flow out of the lung parenchyma but not back in.
definitions.source_excerpt: The Spiration valve is a one-way umbrella-shaped endobronchial valve

clinical_pearls.content: A continuous air leak or increase in the output of air in the waterseal chamber of a pleural fluid collection container should alert the physician to the possibility of a bronchopleural fistula.
clinical_pearls.source_excerpt: A continuous air leak or increase in the output of air in the waterseal chamber of a pleural ﬂuid collection container

clinical_pearls.content: Limiting airway pressure is an important strategy as continued airflow through the tract delays natural healing. Minimization of positive end expiratory pressure (PEEP), inspiratory flow rate, and tidal volume should be attempted to the extent tolerated by the patient.
clinical_pearls.source_excerpt: Limiting airway pres- sure is an important strategy… Minimization of positive end expiratory pressure (PEEP), inspiratory ﬂow rate, and tidal volume should be attempted…

clinical_pearls.content: These results suggest that endobronchial valve placement appears to be a safe and effective intervention for prolonged air leak from various cases.

practice_recommendations.content: Bronchoscopy should be performed in all patients suspected of having a BPF.
practice_recommendations.source_excerpt: Bronchoscopy should be performed in all patients suspected of having a BPF.

practice_recommendations.content: The initial management of any BPF should ﬁrst address any immediate, life-threatening conditions, such as pleural space contamination, pulmonary ﬂooding, or tension pneumothorax. A chest tube, if not already in place, should be inserted immediately to address these concerns.
practice_recommendations.source_excerpt: A chest tube… should be inserted immediately to address these concerns.

practice_recommendations.content: It is recommended to start considering valve removal after 6 weeks after placement o upon resolution of the air leak to minimize long-term airway complications such as infection, valve migration, or tissue hyperplasia and stenosis around the foreign body (valve).
